articles.title: Both blocs claim upper hand in crucial Israeli election | First Thing
articles.summary:
Benjamin Netanyahu vows to form new coalition while opposition bloc leader says result shows prime minister should step down. Plus, a scathing review of Elon Musk’s AI-generated version of The Odyssey

Good morning. Israel could be in for weeks of political haggling after exit polls and partial official results showed neither Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition nor the opposition bloc led by the former general Gadi Eisenkot had won enough seats to form a government.

With 70% of the vote, or 4m ballots, counted so far, the Netanyahu bloc had 54 seats, the Eisenkot-led Change bloc 47 seats, and the Palestinian parties 19 seats. Sixty-one seats are needed for a majority.

What have the two leaders said so far? Israel’s longest-serving prime minister vowed to assemble a coalition through agreements between his Likud party, far-right factions and Jewish religious parties. Eisenkot had said earlier in the evening that “people decided in favour of change” and Netanyahu should have “announced today his retirement from politics”.

What does the increase in the Palestinian bloc mean? The election was marked by a record participation by Israeli citizens of Palestinian origin, a discriminated minority that makes up about 20% of the country’s population. Julian Borger explains from Nazareth that opposition leader Eisenkot will have to work with Arab-Israeli leaders to have a hope of governing. Millions of other Palestinians living under Israeli rule in the occupied West Bank and Gaza cannot vote.

Here is what we know about the declared results so far. Our live coverage continues on the website.

What else has Trump been saying about fossil fuels? Trump suggested on Tuesday that Venezuela would become the 51st US state as the president showed off a tanker he claimed had “1m barrels of oil on it” from the country, nine months after deposing its president.

articles.title: ‘Jewish supremacy is the law of the land’
articles.summary:
‘Jewish supremacy is the law of the land’

Middle East Eye spoke to Antony Loewenstein, an independent journalist, film-maker and author of The Palestine Laboratory, about the Israeli election results.

“There's not really any major or even significant difference between Netanyahu and the so-called opposition on any of the key issues - Iran, Lebanon, Gaza, the West Bank - and in some ways, although at this point it's obviously unclear who won and Netanyahu seems to be slightly ahead with his bloc, but obviously that could change in the coming days or weeks,” Loewenstein told MEE.

“But really what that says, I think, is something much bigger. Which is that a sizeable proportion, if not the majority, of Israeli Jewish voters do not want to engage with Arabs, do not want Arabs in government, do not believe in any self-determination for Arabs, and do not want any real change between the West Bank and Gaza. And in fact a sizeable proportion, if not a majority, want to get rid of all Arabs from Palestine and as many Arabs from Israel itself, which really I think speaks to the fact that the issue in Israel, as many people like me have been saying for years, is not just about Netanyahu.”

“Obviously, it's very significant that the Arab parties have won hugely, and that's probably because many Palestinians voted in Israel, and also probably more left-wing Israelis, including some Israeli Jewish friends of mine who wanted to support the Arab Parties,” he added. 

“And in a sane country, those voters and those parties would have representation in a government, or at least in a sizable opposition. But at this current point it's very hard to see if that will happen because both major parties, the opposition and Netanyahu, have refused doing so. So really it just shows that Jewish supremacy is the law of the land,” Loewenstein concluded.

articles.title: Trump says government to ‘terminate’ Biden-era methane emissions rules
articles.summary:
Critics warn of climate danger as president in Texas claims change will save companies and consumers billions

Donald Trump announced his administration is “terminating” Biden-era regulations holding oil and gas companies accountable for large leaks of planet-warming methane during a rally in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday evening.

Trump said during a campaign rally in Texas that the change would save consumers and energy producers $45bn and unlock 210 million barrels of oil – equivalent to about 10 days of US petroleum consumption. “Tonight, I’m officially terminating Biden’s expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers,” Trump said, lifting what he called “crippling regulations on methane that caused prices to skyrocket” for small oil and gas operators.
